name: Pessimistic Locking Strategies
tagline: Acquiring exclusive or shared row locks upfront with bounded timeouts and canonical lock ordering to serialize high-contention writes.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of pessimistic locking—from `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, `NOWAIT`, and `SKIP LOCKED` to preventing AB-BA deadlocks and pool starvation.

spark.summary: A concurrency control approach that acquires exclusive or shared locks before reading or modifying data, serializing conflicting writers upfront to prevent lost updates.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) with strict lock timeouts and deterministic lock ordering under high contention, or `SKIP LOCKED` for concurrent job queues.

learningJourney.title: What is Pessimistic Locking
learningJourney.explanation:
**Pessimistic Locking** assumes concurrent transactions *will* collide and prevents lost updates by acquiring a lock **before** reading or modifying the target record. In SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB), `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` places an exclusive (`X`) row lock until `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.

Modern engines also provide `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` (Postgres: allows concurrent foreign-key `FOR KEY SHARE` checks), `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` (fail immediately with `SQLSTATE 55P03`), and `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (skip locked rows for multi-worker queues).

learningJourney.title: Why we need Pessimistic Locking (when OCC collapses)
learningJourney.explanation: When hundreds of concurrent buyers target the exact same row—like the last 2 VIP seats on a flight or a hot flash-sale SKU—Optimistic Concurrency Control collapses into a retry storm wasting 80%+ of DB IOPS. Pessimistic locking serializes access at the database lock manager so each writer executes cleanly in turn.

learningJourney.title: Where Pessimistic Locking fits (and where to avoid it)
learningJourney.explanation: Use pessimistic row locks for hot-key serialization, multi-row ledger transfers, and Postgres job queues; avoid holding locks across human think-time or non-indexed scans.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Flash-Sale Inventory & Ledger Transfers
benefits: Prevents retry storms at >15–20% conflict rates and protects multi-row atomic invariants.
costs: Waiters queue behind the lock holder, increasing p99 latency and connection occupancy.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Postgres Job Queues (`SKIP LOCKED`)
benefits: Multiple workers claim distinct pending jobs concurrently with zero lock contention.
costs: Does not guarantee strict FIFO ordering under retries.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Non-Indexed Columns & Long HTTP Think-Time
benefits: Use OCC (`ETag` + `If-Match`) for user-edited forms and ensure `FOR UPDATE` always hits a `UNIQUE` index.
costs: `FOR UPDATE` on a non-indexed column or MySQL `REPEATABLE READ` range locks entire gaps/tables.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Lock Timeouts, Canonical Ordering & `SKIP LOCKED` are managed
learningJourney.explanation: Never leave PostgreSQL's `lock_timeout` at `0` (infinite) or MySQL's `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` at `50s`. Set `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2000ms'` inside an explicit `BEGIN ... COMMIT` block (autocommit releases `FOR UPDATE` immediately and protects nothing!), and sort multi-row lock keys.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Ticketing Seat Hold with `lock_timeout`
learningJourney.explanation: A ticketing checkout service opens a short DB transaction with `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2000ms'`, locks the requested seat rows in ascending `seat_id` order via `FOR UPDATE`, decrements availability, writes an outbox event, and commits in <4 ms—keeping all payment gateway HTTP calls outside the lock.

options.text: Workers immediately skip rows locked by peers and claim distinct batches without blocking on each other
options.feedback: Correct: `SKIP LOCKED` eliminates head-of-line lock waiting across concurrent queue consumers.

options.text: `SKIP LOCKED` guarantees strict global FIFO ordering across all workers
options.feedback: `SKIP LOCKED` trades strict FIFO ordering for non-blocking concurrency.

options.text: `SKIP LOCKED` works without an explicit `BEGIN ... COMMIT` transaction
options.feedback: In autocommit mode, locks release immediately after the SELECT finishes.
